text:
I've never trusted code I didn't review until now.

Agents write more code than any of us can review. We often end up skimming the PR/diff and pushing. Current review methods do not prove the code is correct or does what we asked. Recent research found the best AI code reviewer caught the bug on its first try only 42% of the time.*

The evaluation bottleneck, regressions, and security incidents have forced us to find a better way.

Introducing Proof-Driven Development Kit (PDD Kit) from @MSFTResearch. PDD Kit brings assurance to AI-generated code. You describe what you want to build in plain English. PDD Kit captures your objective, what we call your intent, and uses a verifier tool to prove the code meets it for every possible input.

You never review a single line of the code or the proof. You review your plan and the defined objectives in natural language.

A simple example is login. With testing, you check that only the correct password logs in a user but with a proof on top you can verify that there is no case a wrong password allows login. You can prove correctness and security across many complex scenarios.

Not only does PDD Kit prove the correctness of your code, but also your intent so you can have confidence your code is correct and does what you asked. It provides a level of assurance that specs, code review, and tests never could. PDD Kit is in limited research preview. Video explainer below.

If you want to learn more, I'll be sharing PDD Kit at GitHub Universe next week, Oct 28–29. Swing by the Speakeasy, ask for GitHub Next, and ask me about verified code. If you're in SF, let me know.

*Yang et al., "(When) Should a Software Factory be Lights-off?", Microsoft Research and CMU, Oct 2026

quotedTweet.text:
How do you _guarantee_ your agent's code is correct? You prove it.

Introducing Proof Driven Development Kit (PDD Kit) from @MSFTResearch.

PDD Kit helps turn your plan into a formal spec, then proves the agent's code meets that spec for every input. No vibe verification. PDD Kit is integrated with @GitHubNext's Chopin, so you can plan as a team.

PDD Kit takes an app's login flow from intent to a verified pull request:

It discusses your code, infers your intent as it goes, and proposes a formal spec in Verus, a proof language for Rust.

Once you approve the spec, the Verus verifier automatically proves the code meets it.

Where proof isn't possible, it falls back to empirical verification with tests and computer-use agents (CUAs).

It works on Rust today. No new language, no change in how you produce the underlying code, making formal methods more accessible.

The goal is a verified software factory, where engineers review specifications instead of code.

Come see it in action at GitHub Universe, Oct 28–29. Swing by the Speakeasy and ask for GitHub Next!

🚨Harry Kane on Mikel Arteta closing the line and trying to stop Bayern attack.

🎙️ Reporter: “Harry, Camera caught a moment Arteta closing the line to stop attack. What do you think?”

🗣️ Kane: “Absolutely! I honestly think someone needs to look into this because what Arteta is doing is crossing the line. This is football, not a game where you manipulate every situation and then act like the victim when things don’t go your way.”

“I’m sorry, but Arsenal need to stop behaving like they’re the only honest club in football. Arteta complains about everything, questions every decision, and somehow always wants the entire world to believe his team has been robbed.”

“If the officials find that he has crossed the line, then yes, he should face serious sanctions. A ban, a fine, whatever the rules demand. Nobody should be bigger than the game.”

“Arsenal fans can get angry with me all they want, but they need to ask themselves one question: if another manager behaved exactly like Arteta, would they defend him this passionately?”

🎙️Reporter: “So you’re saying Arsenal fans are part of the problem?”

🗣️ Kane: “I’m saying some of them refuse to see anything wrong with their club. They want respect from everybody, but the moment someone criticises Arteta, suddenly that person is the enemy. That’s not football debate; that’s blind loyalty.”

“If Arsenal want to be respected as champions, they need to stop acting like victims every time someone challenges them.”

Don't be the last one to patch.

text:
my unpopular opinion is that ChatGPT apps are the best distribution play rn

we spent last month shipping these for agency clients and...

+50-200% on income those apps were already doing

just you literally get an access to ~900M weekly users for free

+ you're not struggled with onboarding, since it's built on top of ChatGPT and for user who never used your product, much easier to get in via gpt interface

same product, same pricing, just new way of using your product

and the fear that OpenAI just clones you is backwards

cloning your niche is the ONE move that costs them more than it returns...

they'd rather buy you and ship it out of the box

here's exactly how to launch it:

1. pick a workflow the client already gets paid for

> not a new idea
> an existing paid workflow with proven demand

2. build it as an MCP server

> streamable HTTP on public HTTPS, usually at /mcp
> that server is the whole product surface
> UI is optional, tools come first

3. name and describe every tool like the model is reading it, because it is

> action-oriented name, a human title, a description of when to use it
> accurate annotations and a real input schema
> that metadata is what decides whether you get called at all

4. add the UI after the tools already work

> expose it as an MCP resource with a ui:// uri
> set the type to text/html;profile=mcp-app
> your built js gets inlined into that resource and runs in an iframe

5. connect it at https://t.co/gtoWZaeDWZ and break it yourself

> plus button, add custom MCP server
> paste the url with /mcp, create as a plugin
> run MCP Inspector first and catch the schema errors there

6. submit at https://t.co/fXGl4AJRkL and overprepare

> a zip of the built plugin and publisher verification
> a privacy policy url, no privacy policy means no review
> 5 positive and 3 negative test cases
> release notes and a demo video for the reviewer
> a domain token hosted at /.well-known/openai-apps-challenge

7. keep billing on YOUR backend

> OAuth 2.1 into the account system you already have
> enforce authorization on every request, not through the model
> there is no revenue share
> the plugin is the channel and the MRR stays yours

that's absolutely free traffic and by some reason most of products skip it...

the guy below is a good case which shows real efficiency of this approach (he literally made around +$40k monthly income)

有一次，孙哥携带我，和朋友们一起就餐。
在大家纷纷起身，觥筹交错，举杯畅饮之际。
他的敌蜜假装不经意地问：“孙哥，你多高。”
想要一举击溃孙哥。

没想到，孙哥居然面不改色地回答：“我1米75。”
我不可置信地看着他，那一瞬间，第一次体会到了来自爱人的背刺。

我以为爱情是两个人共同面对世界，没想到关键时刻，他竟然选择了独自长高。

“那你呢”客户问。
我看了看眼神坚毅的孙哥，为了爱情，我只好说，“我1米66。”

爱情的忠贞就在于此，
像险峰，增加你的高度，衬托你的威仪。
不仅爱你伟岸的身躯， 也爱你坚持的位置，足下的鞋垫。

“I just smiled and told one of them, 'Keep that same energy when we score.' He didn't seem to appreciate that very much.”

LayerFS v1.0.0 is out 🎉 Open-source (MIT) 

Recursive filesystem for AI  agents.

6 core ideas:

1. Ephemeral computing: agents spend ~80% thinking, so each Bash call mounts a Workspace, then commits
2. Decentralized agents: every agent commits to one Store, no DB server
3. Multiagent coordination: every tool call is a Commit; same-file clashes refused
4. Recursive filesystem: forks copy no files, at any depth
5. Ultra storage: dedup, then compression: 10 copies → 0.31
6. Instant bootstrap: ignored files stay in every Commit. ~5 min install vs 0.05 s mount

And 4 more:

7. Auto checkpoints: fork from any step
8. Append-only objects: content-addressed, never rewritten
9. .lww: lockfiles and caches take the newest edit
10. Big file, small edit: a write keeps only its bytes

Here are our links:

text:
2011年，谷歌前CEO埃里克·施密特，开始和一个叫 Cami Clark 的年轻女创业者交往。

她来自内华达州里诺的蓝领家庭。
刚到湾区时没什么人脉，靠自己在 TED 活动上一个个认识人。
这段关系，维持了大约三年。

后来她做了第二家公司，施密特投了一小笔钱。公司最终没做起来。
但那份融资材料上，还列着一位顾问："Dr. Dario Amodei"。
那时，他还是斯坦福的一名博士后。

一份失败的融资材料上，同时写着她的前任，和她的下一任。

2014年，她和阿莫迪在一起了。
施密特没有从她的生活里消失。
2018年，他去两人在旧金山的公寓做客，对这个年轻科学家的想法印象很深。
2020年12月，阿莫迪和几位同事离开 OpenAI，创办 Anthropic。
要钱，也要一个够分量的名字。
她想到了一个人。

2021年2月，她给施密特发了一份40页的方案：成立一只"AGI之母基金"，正式确立她在 Anthropic 的角色，并由她管理施密特的股份。
方案在 Anthropic 内部遭到反对。施密特最后绕开基金，直接投资。
那一年，Anthropic 的A轮融资是 1.24亿美元，施密特是参与者之一。
第二年，她和阿莫迪结了婚。

五年后。
2026年10月，彭博报道：施密特持有 Anthropic 约 1% 的股份，有望在上市时迎来最大的个人回报之一。
按投资人讨论的 1.5万亿美元 估值，这1%约值 150亿美元。
如果冲到2万亿，就是 200亿。
当年那几千万美元，翻了几百倍。

而那个牵线的人——
据报道，她在 Anthropic 没有任何正式职位。她曾想拿公司股份，被其他联合创始人否了。
当然，她也没吃亏。
她嫁的那位CEO，个人身家估计约155亿美元。

这个故事告诉我们：
分手可以，别拉黑。 你永远不知道，哪位前任会成为你老公的天使投资人。

（这不是搜索引擎偶然出错，而是刻意为之的结果。👇）

text:
这可能是 Delphi Digital 最近最好的一篇长文：《庄家通吃：为什么投机是未来十年的主题》。

小编看完觉得，重点并不在于它投研了什么新赛道，更像是一种姿态和明示：

别再装价值投资了，大方承认“投机”就是这个时代的刚需。而在一个全民皆赌的时代，最聪明的策略不是去牌桌上挑筹码，你最好直接买下赌场本身。

文章里几个非常刺骨的洞察，以及大量值得细品的数据：

1. 为什么所有人都在赌？因为“正常路径”已经失效

历史上的投机大多由两种引擎驱动：
a.新技术带来的“基建狂热”，如当年的铁路、现在的 AI；
b.阶层固化和法币贬值逼出来的“彩票绝望”,赌一把算了。

而现在，这两个引擎在历史上首次同时全速运转。

对年轻人来说，靠打工存钱买房的传统社会契约已经破产；目前美国首次购房者的中位年龄创下了 40 岁的历史新高，占购房比例降至历史最低的 21%。

存 0 块钱和存 1 万块钱毫无区别，因为都付不起首付。所以，去期权市场、预测市场和土狗盘里博一个 100 倍，成了年轻人在数学上唯一合理的突围方式。

数据显示，80% 冲向高风险资产的 Z 世代坦言，这么做是因为“感觉自己在财务上掉队了”；

过去一年，36% 的 30 岁以下美国年轻男性参与过体育博彩，35 岁以下投资者中有 43% 交易过期权。

2. AI 是生产力，更是最大的“逼赌机器”

这是全文最反直觉的视角。我们总以为 AI 是用来投资的，但报告指出，AI 正在全方位把普通人逼向赌桌。

text:
看完有点心疼，同作为母亲，极度共情妈妈，想给贝塔一个大大的拥抱。

工作中见过不少父母和孩子走向对立的情况，所以特别能理解这种拉扯。孩子对独立的渴望是真实的，多数家长都要面对：如何在保护与独立之间找到过渡，同时不把亲子关系彻底推向对立。

“永远不会原谅”“你是世上最坏的妈妈”这些话，是高度情绪化的反应，不是永久标签，妈妈不用太担心。当下先接纳情绪，再谈规则。让孩子参与讨论什么可以做、什么不能做、违反会怎样、怎样才能获得更多自由。11岁已经可以表达意见，完全被排除在决策之外时，抵触只会更强。

他冲出门又怕黑折返，说明情绪很大但还没完全失控。我十四五岁离家出走时，走了好几里脚底磨出泡也没回头，流浪了一星期才回家。相比之下，他还是有分寸的。

这个阶段最容易把“保护”和“控制”混在一起。孩子感受到的往往是“你不信任我”，而不是“你在保护我”。

妈妈放心，孩子心里明白你是爱他的，也想保护他，只是节奏错位了。事后如果愿意开放沟通、认真修复，彼此都会更理解对方的需求和边界。一切都会慢慢变好的。祝福🙏

昨晚真的是很伤心，X也不想刷，觉也没睡好。

起因是儿子偷偷开了个油管账号。

上周他提过，被我明确拒绝了。他只有 11 岁，讲话还经常颠三倒四，让他拥有独立账号，无异于让稚童在网络江湖里裸奔。我给了他一个大写的“不”，他也答应了。

结果昨晚我发现，他还是偷偷摸摸开了。我的生气可想而知：一来气他阳奉阴违，二来担忧他那远超心智支撑水平的强烈独立意志。

我让他删掉，并警告若有下次，将罚他一周不许碰游戏卡。

他就失控了。他说第一条视频才面世不到十分钟就被我删了，他永远不会原谅我。他说他就是想要一个属于自己的油管账号，碍着谁了？

我说：“不是碍着谁，是你还太小，不知江湖险恶。况且油管规定 13 岁以下不能拥有独立账号。”

妹妹在一旁补刀：“那个瑞恩，6 岁就有自己的账号了呀。”（瑞恩是油管网红，小小年纪身价千万，女儿常看他的视频。）

我说：“那是他爸爸妈妈在经营，他只是个演员。”

女儿：“那你帮哥哥经营好不好？”

我还没来得及反驳，儿子倒先忍不住了：“我就想要一个自己的账号，谁也不能碰的那种！”

那就是绝对的红线了。我坚决不同意，逼他当面删掉了。

他满面泪痕，说我是世上最坏的妈妈。他说他此刻万念俱灰，不想在这个家待了。

大晚上，个位数温度，他真的外套都没穿，拉开门就朝外冲。直到走到后院石阶，看着黑黢黢的树林，才折回来说“忘拿东西了”，跑回房间睡了。

我却在黑暗的客厅里坐了很久，感到伤心、挫败与无助。

我不明白，这种明文规定的红线，利弊讲了千百遍，为什么就是不能让他接受，甚至闹到要离家出走？他现在是怕黑折返了，可过几年等他长大了，是不是真的会带着“我妈妈是世上最坏的妈妈”的念头，彻底离开？

以前和婆婆聊起我家以前的房客（一个单亲爸爸带三个十几岁小孩），我说：“我没法理解，为什么妈妈会放弃孩子的抚养权。” 婆婆说：“有些孩子到了青春期，会把妈妈气到七窍生烟，巴不得离他们越远越好。”

在他 11 岁的这个夜晚，我有点理解了。

他还是小婴儿的时候，折腾得我日夜难眠，可那时我常顶着黑眼圈遐想：以后他找女朋友，一定要集齐所有美好的品质，要是敢对他不好，我第一个不饶。

现在的想法却是：只希望未来的那个女孩能包容他的坏脾气，这就足够了。

昨晚真的是很伤心，X也不想刷，觉也没睡好。

起因是儿子偷偷开了个油管账号。

上周他提过，被我明确拒绝了。他只有 11 岁，讲话还经常颠三倒四，让他拥有独立账号，无异于让稚童在网络江湖里裸奔。我给了他一个大写的“不”，他也答应了。

结果昨晚我发现，他还是偷偷摸摸开了。我的生气可想而知：一来气他阳奉阴违，二来担忧他那远超心智支撑水平的强烈独立意志。

我让他删掉，并警告若有下次，将罚他一周不许碰游戏卡。

他就失控了。他说第一条视频才面世不到十分钟就被我删了，他永远不会原谅我。他说他就是想要一个属于自己的油管账号，碍着谁了？

我说：“不是碍着谁，是你还太小，不知江湖险恶。况且油管规定 13 岁以下不能拥有独立账号。”

妹妹在一旁补刀：“那个瑞恩，6 岁就有自己的账号了呀。”（瑞恩是油管网红，小小年纪身价千万，女儿常看他的视频。）

我说：“那是他爸爸妈妈在经营，他只是个演员。”

女儿：“那你帮哥哥经营好不好？”

我还没来得及反驳，儿子倒先忍不住了：“我就想要一个自己的账号，谁也不能碰的那种！”

那就是绝对的红线了。我坚决不同意，逼他当面删掉了。

他满面泪痕，说我是世上最坏的妈妈。他说他此刻万念俱灰，不想在这个家待了。

大晚上，个位数温度，他真的外套都没穿，拉开门就朝外冲。直到走到后院石阶，看着黑黢黢的树林，才折回来说“忘拿东西了”，跑回房间睡了。

我却在黑暗的客厅里坐了很久，感到伤心、挫败与无助。

我不明白，这种明文规定的红线，利弊讲了千百遍，为什么就是不能让他接受，甚至闹到要离家出走？他现在是怕黑折返了，可过几年等他长大了，是不是真的会带着“我妈妈是世上最坏的妈妈”的念头，彻底离开？

以前和婆婆聊起我家以前的房客（一个单亲爸爸带三个十几岁小孩），我说：“我没法理解，为什么妈妈会放弃孩子的抚养权。” 婆婆说：“有些孩子到了青春期，会把妈妈气到七窍生烟，巴不得离他们越远越好。”

在他 11 岁的这个夜晚，我有点理解了。

他还是小婴儿的时候，折腾得我日夜难眠，可那时我常顶着黑眼圈遐想：以后他找女朋友，一定要集齐所有美好的品质，要是敢对他不好，我第一个不饶。

现在的想法却是：只希望未来的那个女孩能包容他的坏脾气，这就足够了。

text:
「Claude」多开 Pro 还是升 Max，我的建议看用量

先看价格：Pro 每月 20 刀；Max 5x 100 刀，用量是 Pro 的 5 倍；Max 20x 200 刀，用量是 Pro 的 20 倍，另送每月 200 刀 API 额度（都不含税）

用量不大、100 刀够用，又怕封：注册 3 到 5 个 Pro，用工具切换。5 个 Pro 正好 100 刀，用量和 Max 5x 一样，还不用过 KYC

切号工具按场景选：

1. Claude Code 命令行、VS Code 插件：claude-swap，开源，每个号 cswap add 存一次，之后一条命令切，不用退出登录
2. 想要图形界面：Orca，多个 Claude 号一键切，正在跑的会话也能切
3. 网页版：Chrome 开几个用户，或者装 SessionBox 插件，一个号一个窗口
4. 不装工具：VS Code 插件登一个号，Claude 桌面客户端登另一个

原帖说的 CC Switch，评论区有人说目前还切不了 Claude 官方订阅，Codex 可以。claude-swap 有到限额前自动换号的功能，建议别开，评论区有人说绕 5 小时额度最容易封。手动切号也要看清当前是哪个号，有人切错直接封了一个

切号后记得新建会话，别一个会话里混着几个号的数据，容易关联封号

Pro 风控很小，只要 IP 干净、只有自己用、不多人共用，基本风险不大

用量大的，就搏一搏 KYC。过了也可能封，不过封了又如何，换 IP 继续注册，大佬们都是 20 个号起步

炒股软件居然也搞开源了，这操作属实有点离谱。

OpenStock 在 GitHub 上 star 已经 16900+，一个开源项目，把付费行情软件里那些要收你钱的功能，全给塞进一个免费平台，还放话永久免费。

它想干的事特别直接：一分钱不掏，也能用上一整套看盘工具。我拆开给你说：

1️⃣ 实时股价，行情随时盯着

2️⃣ TradingView 的 K 线，专业软件同款

3️⃣ 技术指标，该有的都有

4️⃣ Reddit、X、财经新闻、Polymarket 的市场情绪，全揉进一个界面，省得你开一堆网页来回切

最让我买账的是 Watchlist 这块。把持仓加进去，Gemini 会顺着你关注的方向，每天生成一份 AI 新闻摘要，直接推到你邮箱。

说白了，盯盘、看新闻、刷情绪、整理信息流这些事，它基本都给你捏一块儿了，一个界面搞定。

技术栈也不含糊，Next.js、TypeScript、MongoDB，还挂着 GitHub Trending 当日第一的牌子，不是那种随手写完就扔的玩具。

不过我得提一句，它自己也讲了，OpenStock 是社区搭起来的，不是券商，行情数据可能有延迟，里面的东西也不构成任何投资建议，你自己心里有数就行。

想上手的自己去扒源码：

🔗 https://t.co/z836jbyUdO

为什么我认为，今天的欧洲，本质上就是一个穿着高定西装、端着红酒杯的福利版大清。

如果把19世纪的晚清和如今的欧洲放在一起对比刨析，你会发现这两者的病灶、心态和衰弱的剧本都一模一样。

何出此言，论据如下：

其一，欧洲把道德与合规当成天朝礼法，把中美科技看作奇技淫巧

当年乾隆和晚清士大夫面对英国的蒸汽机、火车和洋枪洋炮，第一反应不是恐慌，而是居高临下的道德鄙视，认为那是毫无教化的奇技淫巧，只有大清的孔孟礼治才是人类文明的最高形态。

今天的欧洲老爷看中美，心态一模一样。

他们打心底里瞧不起硅谷的野蛮生长的科技新贵，更瞧不起中国没日没夜卷出来的超级供应链。

在欧洲老爷们眼里，中美这是没有灵魂的野蛮内卷，只有欧洲高举的环保主义、数据隐私、多元平权和每周35小时工作制，才是人类文明的天朝礼法。

他们沉溺在道德审美上的优越感里，用文明裁判的姿态掩盖自己在生产力上的全面阳痿。

其二，欧洲的奢侈品和燃油车，就是当代的茶叶、丝绸与瓷器

大清曾经靠着农业文明攒下的极致老底，茶叶、丝绸、瓷器，赚走了全球大量的白银，甚至狂妄地认为外国人不喝大清的茶叶就会便秘而死。

欧洲过去几十年吃的老本，本质上就是工业2.0时代攒下的茶叶和瓷器，包括法国的LV与爱马仕、德国的BBA燃油车与精密阀门、瑞士的手表与医药。

欧洲人同样产生了一种致命的幻觉：

认为无论科技怎么改变，中美的新贵们永远得排队买欧洲的皮包和机械，欧洲永远可以靠着祖传的品牌溢价和专利护城河，躺着收割全世界的财富。

直到中国出现的新能源车直接打穿德国汽车工业的底裤、AI 的兴起开始重构工业软件与研发范式，欧洲才惊觉自己的丝绸瓷器不再是不可替代的硬通货了。

其三，布鲁塞尔的罚单经济，就是当年的广州十三行

大清闭关锁国，但又馋洋人的白银，怎么办？

搞出了一套广州十三行体制：

自己不搞工业、不搞航海，就在通商口岸设卡，制定最繁琐的规矩，向外国商人征收高昂的规礼银和买路钱。

今天欧盟总部的布鲁塞尔，正是数字时代的广州十三行。

自己孵化不出OpenAI、英伟达、字节跳动，就写全世界最厚的《AI法案》和《数字市场法案》。

你美国科技巨头想进欧洲4.5亿人的市场？

可以，先按我的规矩交几十亿欧元的反垄断罚单。

用行政设卡和司法敲诈来代替产业竞争，结果把真正的创新者全挡在门外，把自己彻底锁死在旧时代。

其四，从入关八旗退化成提笼架鸟的铁杆庄稼

满清八旗刚入关时（对应欧洲的大航海和早期工业革命），那也是敢拼命、敢流血的凶悍战力。

但承平日久，八旗子弟拿上了国家包养的铁杆庄稼（世袭俸禄），迅速退化成只会提笼架鸟、抽大烟、听戏的寄生阶层。

到了晚清财政破产，朝廷哪怕敢克扣一点点旗饷，八旗兵不打洋人，先在京城闹事。

今天欧洲的高福利选民，就是当代的八旗子弟。

二战后几代人吃尽了工业霸权的红利，把高福利、长休假、终身不解雇当成了天经地义的铁杆庄稼。

现在老本吃光了，法国国债飙到GDP的120%，政府刚想砍610亿欧元预算自救，这群平时连班都不愿多加的当代旗人立刻冲上街头，把143年历史的市政厅烧成灰烬。

其五，既得利益死保风水，把每一次洋务运动扼杀在摇篮里

晚清不是没有明白人，李鸿章、曾国藩也想搞洋务运动，也想修铁路、架电线。

但为什么搞不成？

Here's my updated review of each personal agent:

1. Grok Bot

Pros: A team of bots is the easiest to understand. Free X access is amazing for research. Voice mode and the new Pages feature are great.

Cons: Email feature doesn't really work.

2. Muse

Pros: Free, best consumer UX, most meme-worthy avatar, and business calling is amazing.

Cons: Muse Wonder is good but Opus/Astra is better.

3. Claude Duet

Pros: Most proactive out of the box. Feels polished and simple to use. Arguably the best model behind it.

Cons: Missing some features in research preview, like being able to drive its browser.

4. ChatGPT Dots

Pros: Works inside ChatGPT, so it can drive all your cloud and local threads.

Cons: Much better than at launch but still buggy. Voice mode is slow to connect.

I've also tried Instinct and some of the other agents, but I don't want more than 4 at a time connected to my email.

📌 Don't miss my full Claude Duet review here for everything that it can do: https://t.co/EK28ETwWjD

一对夫妻带着小孩乘坐大巴回乡途中

因孩子肚子饿、不断吵闹，夫妇无奈中途下车，在附近快餐店吃了点东西。  

吃饱喝足后，餐厅电视播报新闻：就在刚才，一辆乡间巴士被山上落石击中，全车人员无一生还。

仔细一看，正是他们刚才搭乘的那班车。  

看着新闻，妻子喃喃道：“要是刚才我们没有下车就好了”  

丈夫怒道：“说什么傻话！要是没下车……”  话音未落，他也懂了妻子话中之意。

text:
Google 开源了一个 Agent，能直接操作安卓手机，连 App 测试都能自己跑。

项目叫 ARTEMIS。

通过 MCP 接入 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor 等工具，就能让 AI：

自动点击、滑动、输入，跨 App 完成任务
测试登录、页面跳转等完整流程
自动抓取截图、Logcat 日志，辅助定位 Bug
生成测试报告，支持执行回放

提供两种模式：

Flash：约 3–5 秒执行一步，适合日常操作。
Pro：多 Agent 协作，带计划、执行检查和结果验证。

项目公布的 AndroidWorld 测试完成率超过 99%。

最实用的是：以前写完 App 还得自己拿手机反复点，现在可以把这部分工作交给 Agent。

目前主要支持 Android，iOS 还在规划中。

GitHub：https://t.co/LTGQOFPtsX

#AI #Agent #ClaudeCode #Codex #Android #OpenSource

Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. 

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.

Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. 

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.

text:
你还记得 Google Reader 吗？

我 08 年就是它的重度用户。13 年它关了，我开始到处找替代品：Feedly、Inoreader，还有 Mac 上很漂亮的 Reeder，都用过，但总差点意思。

后来用 Readwise 收集阅读书签，它推出 Readwise Reader 后，我就把订阅都搬了过去。再后来 AI 火了，我把源切到开源的 RSS 上，让 AI 先做一遍简单解读，再推送到我的 Telegram。

为什么一直这么折腾？

因为我不想打开某个网站去看它的推荐榜单。人一旦掉进信息茧房，就很难看到茧房外面的世界。自己挑的源，至少知道信息是从哪来的。

还有件挺开心的事：当年在 Google Reader 里订阅的那批优秀博主，现在好多都在推特上又遇到了，身边还多了不少新的好作者。

平台一直在变，但值得订阅的，始终是那些有深度思考、愿意表达的人。

听闻某单位一男同事，刚进单位一年有余，因帅气高大，期间班中女同学表白无数，以至于后来陆续发生关系，

酒桌上得意吐槽，曾一龙三凤快乐于实验器材室，一龙二凤快乐于杂物间，一碗家常面片儿约会其他班花季少女于周末家中欢愉，

上班两年期间，其御女数量甚为可观，收到的小礼物，小手工，书信表白无数，加微信者每日平均5-8人，更有甚者，与中年妇女和上级单位职员，以及本单位的外地女，保持关系，深夜为其买药，送饭，吆来喝去，甚是得意，

最后东窗事发，如过街老鼠一般，传闻其得罪了单位大佬的小蜜，结局甚是难堪，

据说，今时今日仍在保险公司，娱乐场所等地，续写他那传奇欲望的人生……

text:
刚刚的柏林GTC大会上，英伟达CEO黄仁勋的主题演讲刚进行到四分之一，台下几人突然站起来打断他，冲着台上喊话，抗议英伟达硬件出现在乌克兰战场的俄罗斯无人机里。

当时黄仁勋正在台上展示已经全面投产的新一代Vera Rubin计算机，介绍这台机器没有一根线缆、采用百分之百液冷，组装时间从以前的两个小时缩短到了五分钟以内。

据报道，台下的抗议者就在这时站起来高喊：“黄仁勋，在俄罗斯无人机里找到的那些技术，你怎么说？那些是英伟达的芯片。你们打算怎么办？”
他们手里拉开的横幅上写着：“英伟达，把你的脏生意收拾干净。”

乌克兰军方此前在击落的俄罗斯无人机里，确实找到过英伟达的Jetson Orin嵌入式模块。
按照现有的制裁规定，俄罗斯原本根本不该拿到这种硬件。

面对突然闹起来的会场，黄仁勋在台上回应说，这都是重要的问题，我们可以回头再聊，但今天现场坐满了人，全球还有一百场观看活动、一万五千人正看着直播，得先让我把演讲做完。

冲突刚发生时，黄仁勋对着现场保安说：“没事，动作轻点，给她个机会，每个人都有说话的机会。”
紧接着，抗议者手里的横幅就被当场没收，人也被直接请出了会场。

text:
大学时，我追一个姑娘，最后却跟她闺蜜谈上了。

这事说起来，得怪我当年自作聪明。

我喜欢的那个姑娘漂亮，但看着不太好接近。我琢磨了半天，决定先跟她室友混熟，让人家帮我说说好话，再找机会约她出来。

她那个室友看着挺单纯，跟谁都笑呵呵的。我就隔三差五找她聊天，请她喝奶茶，想着先在她这儿留下个好印象。

可相处着相处着，情况就不对了。

她室友们开始起哄，连我原本想追的姑娘，都笑着问我们什么时候在一起。

我总不能当场解释：“别误会，我对你好，是想让你帮我追别人。”

何况那姑娘确实好相处。约她吃饭，她会来；跟她说点什么，她都听得认真。见到我时，隔老远就开始笑。

后来，我们就真的谈上了。没有谁正式表白，好像周围人都认定了，我俩也默认了。

毕业后，她继续读研，我找工作。地方离得不算远，见面却越来越少。学生有学生的安排，上班的人也总说忙，联系慢慢淡下来，谁也没认真提过分手。

偏巧，我和当年喜欢的那个姑娘，通过校招进了同一家公司。

这下不用费心找机会，几乎天天都能见面，中午一起吃饭，闲了也会聊几句。

她还是很好看，脾气也没我想象中那么冷。

可我已经没有当初那股劲儿了。跟她坐在一起，就像跟其他同事吃饭，吃完了各自回去上班，也不会再琢磨，她今天是不是多看了我一眼。

反倒偶尔会想起另一个姑娘。

想起她接过奶茶时的表情，想起一群人起哄，她站在旁边笑，也不解释。

一晃，十几年过去了。

有时候想起大学，我还挺怀念那会儿的她，觉得她当时真好骗，我不过多陪她聊聊天，她就跟我走了。

直到前几天晚上。

九点多，闺女作业还没写完，坐在桌前哭。老婆拿着试卷，讲一遍不会，再讲一遍还是不会，气得直拍桌子。

我听见动静，赶紧退出游戏，拿块抹布开始擦桌子，尽量显得自己一直在忙。

老婆忽然扭头问我：“你是不是又在心里觉得，孩子这么笨，都是随我？”

我连忙说没有。

她冷笑一声：“你聪明，你多聪明啊。”

我没敢接话。

她又说：“大学那会儿，一天给你带杯奶茶，没多久你就跟着我跑了。你还真以为自己挺难追呢？”

这事说起来，得怪我当年自作聪明。

我喜欢的那个姑娘漂亮，但看着不太好接近。我琢磨了半天，决定先跟她室友混熟，让人家帮我说说好话，再找机会约她出来。

她那个室友看着挺单纯，跟谁都笑呵呵的。我就隔三差五找她聊天，请她喝奶茶，想着先在她这儿留下个好印象。

可相处着相处着，情况就不对了。

她室友们开始起哄，连我原本想追的姑娘，都笑着问我们什么时候在一起。

我总不能当场解释：“别误会，我对你好，是想让你帮我追别人。”

何况那姑娘确实好相处。约她吃饭，她会来；跟她说点什么，她都听得认真。见到我时，隔老远就开始笑。

后来，我们就真的谈上了。没有谁正式表白，好像周围人都认定了，我俩也默认了。

毕业后，她继续读研，我找工作。地方离得不算远，见面却越来越少。学生有学生的安排，上班的人也总说忙，联系慢慢淡下来，谁也没认真提过分手。

偏巧，我和当年喜欢的那个姑娘，通过校招进了同一家公司。

这下不用费心找机会，几乎天天都能见面，中午一起吃饭，闲了也会聊几句。

她还是很好看，脾气也没我想象中那么冷。

可我已经没有当初那股劲儿了。跟她坐在一起，就像跟其他同事吃饭，吃完了各自回去上班，也不会再琢磨，她今天是不是多看了我一眼。

反倒偶尔会想起另一个姑娘。

想起她接过奶茶时的表情，想起一群人起哄，她站在旁边笑，也不解释。

一晃，十几年过去了。

有时候想起大学，我还挺怀念那会儿的她，觉得她当时真好骗，我不过多陪她聊聊天，她就跟我走了。

直到前几天晚上。

九点多，闺女作业还没写完，坐在桌前哭。老婆拿着试卷，讲一遍不会，再讲一遍还是不会，气得直拍桌子。

我听见动静，赶紧退出游戏，拿块抹布开始擦桌子，尽量显得自己一直在忙。

老婆忽然扭头问我：“你是不是又在心里觉得，孩子这么笨，都是随我？”

我连忙说没有。

她冷笑一声：“你聪明，你多聪明啊。”

我没敢接话。

她又说：“大学那会儿，一天给你带杯奶茶，没多久你就跟着我跑了。你还真以为自己挺难追呢？”

text:
我刚还在看 Claude Duet 怎么按着对手摩擦，结果网友顺着代码底座往下深扒了一层，挖出来一个更炸裂的事实。Grok Bot 底子里跑的是 Opus 5.5，而刚刚发布的 Claude Duet，跑的也是同一个 Opus 5.5。

我说实话看到这我也懵了。
这特么演的是哪出？表面上看是两家巨头在应用层打得头破血流，结果把衣服一扒，里面套着的居然是完完全全同一个大脑。

你说凭什么？大家搬好小板凳以为看的是华山论剑，搞了半天是同一个人换了两身马甲在台上自己扇自己耳光，这不是扯淡吗？

真正离谱的是后面。
再往下拆这盘棋的算力底座，你会发现这帮硅谷大厂的关系网已经彻底乱成了一锅粥。现在的局面是，Anthropic 借着 SpaceXSI 的算力，在市场上跟另一个自己（套壳 Opus 5.5 的 Grok Bot）左右互搏，同时还要腾出手来一起围殴 OpenAI。

为什么这帮向来眼高于顶的巨头，现在连这种近乎精神分裂的牌局都肯坐下来打？

我想了很久，发现AI圈子卷到现在，早就没有什么纯粹的阵营洁癖了。

你以为商战还是以前那种你死我活、老死不相往来的独木桥对决？其实到了算力和模型双双卡脖子的深水区，谁手里有现成的顶尖大脑，谁家里有富余的算力机房，大家为了抢时间窗口直接就拼在一块儿了。

剥开来看，这种敵我同源的奇观，本质上是一场算力换大脑的极限合谋，我管这叫同核互搏局。

你可以这么理解，这就像街上两家吵得最凶的网红火锅店，天天在门口拉横幅骂对方不正宗，结果你绕到后巷一看，两家店不仅共用同一个中央厨房的底料大锅，连烧火的煤气罐都是对门老板支援的。

只要能把街对面的老对手挤下牌桌，现在的巨头根本不在乎自己赚的是台前吆喝的钱，还是后厨卖汤底的钱。

看着这帮科技巨头在台前幕后玩这种排列组合，确实觉得这个行业已经疯魔了。

我但转念一想，这对咱们普通用户反而是件大好事。我给自己定的规矩是，既然Grok Bot和Claude Duet底下塞的都是同一颗Opus 5.5的心脏，咱们完全不用纠结站哪边的队，哪家的交互顺手、哪家的额度便宜，咱们就去薅哪家的羊毛。

看清后厨的底牌，咱们踏踏实实用好手里的工具，剩下的神仙乱炖就让他们自己折腾去吧。

result.text:
我刚还在看 Claude Duet 怎么按着对手摩擦，结果网友顺着代码底座往下深扒了一层，挖出来一个更炸裂的事实。Grok Bot 底子里跑的是 Opus 5.5，而刚刚发布的 Claude Duet，跑的也是同一个 Opus 5.5。

我说实话看到这我也懵了。
这特么演的是哪出？表面上看是两家巨头在应用层打得头破血流，结果把衣服一扒，里面套着的居然是完完全全同一个大脑。

你说凭什么？大家搬好小板凳以为看的是华山论剑，搞了半天是同一个人换了两身马甲在台上自己扇自己耳光，这不是扯淡吗？

真正离谱的是后面。
再往下拆这盘棋的算力底座，你会发现这帮硅谷大厂的关系网已经彻底乱成了一锅粥。现在的局面是，Anthropic 借着 SpaceXSI 的算力，在市场上跟另一个自己（套壳 Opus 5.5 的 Grok Bot）左右互搏，同时还要腾出手来一起围殴 OpenAI。

为什么这帮向来眼高于顶的巨头，现在连这种近乎精神分裂的牌局都肯坐下来打？

我想了很久，发现AI圈子卷到现在，早就没有什么纯粹的阵营洁癖了。

你以为商战还是以前那种你死我活、老死不相往来的独木桥对决？其实到了算力和模型双双卡脖子的深水区，谁手里有现成的顶尖大脑，谁家里有富余的算力机房，大家为了抢时间窗口直接就拼在一块儿了。

剥开来看，这种敵我同源的奇观，本质上是一场算力换大脑的极限合谋，我管这叫同核互搏局。

你可以这么理解，这就像街上两家吵得最凶的网红火锅店，天天在门口拉横幅骂对方不正宗，结果你绕到后巷一看，两家店不仅共用同一个中央厨房的底料大锅，连烧火的煤气罐都是对门老板支援的。

只要能把街对面的老对手挤下牌桌，现在的巨头根本不在乎自己赚的是台前吆喝的钱，还是后厨卖汤底的钱。

看着这帮科技巨头在台前幕后玩这种排列组合，确实觉得这个行业已经疯魔了。

我但转念一想，这对咱们普通用户反而是件大好事。我给自己定的规矩是，既然Grok Bot和Claude Duet底下塞的都是同一颗Opus 5.5的心脏，咱们完全不用纠结站哪边的队，哪家的交互顺手、哪家的额度便宜，咱们就去薅哪家的羊毛。

看清后厨的底牌，咱们踏踏实实用好手里的工具，剩下的神仙乱炖就让他们自己折腾去吧。

事情已经很清楚了

中国至少空置了15GW的机房，这些都是听信国产芯片即将出炉，贷款建的，结果华为之流没法量产，全空在那里

15GW按每MW ¥2亿的建设和维护成本，至少积压了3万亿资金

如果全买B300，需要90万台，中国三年来走私不过3万台左右、机房空转、没有卡，间接损失在10万亿以上

所以政府和银行全慌了，这是🆚恒大更大的雷

这就可以理解、为什么互联网巨头出面买300万Pro 5500，据说订单是600万

这可以让至少6GW机房转起来，这雷先不爆

5500这种美国18岁就能买的消费级卡，性能怎么样不管了，先填坑再说

但是低端芯片不可能有这么多备货，NVDA说可以先卖50万片、其他爱莫能助

那就完了，国内这十万亿的坑迟早要爆

习主席，该壮士断腕了，把任正非之流抛出来、斩首以谢天下

不是这等祸国殃民之徒，不会让中国科技一步步走入这般绝境的

quotedTweet.text:
最开始关注@MaiYangAI，是看到他在小红书发的GrokBot线下活动照片，在x上搜索了还真有，多个平台分发还挺重要的！

其实 Mai 很早就是 SpaceXAI 的推广大使了，当时GrokBot 刚刚降价到达了普通人能接受的心理门槛，但介绍这块内容并不多，然而Youtube很多国外博主又都开始讲，让我的好奇心拉满，所以先发优势也挺重要的！现在讲GrokBot的人越来越多，我其实就记住三个人！

另外，我也是播客学习者，成功不能复制，但可以近距离观察顶级思维的人是如何思考做事的？对自己提升很快！

能把自己看到的做成双语视频发出来的人，真的是有分享精神的！观察他的x增长，虽然不是被大爆款堆砌来的，但一步一个脚印看着很踏实，也不怕哪天突然停更！

我的思考总结：
1、要多平台分发。
2、线上朋友多帮忙，线下志同道合的人多相聚！
3、新产品出现需深耕、占据先发优势。
4、多从人物播客学习、也做利他分享。

quotedTweet.text:
快 2027 年了，我越来越觉得，单纯会开发 Agent，真的不算什么竞争力了。

现在 AI 圈有个特别割裂的现象。

一边是大家天天讨论最新的 Agent 框架、MCP、Skills、多智能体协作，恨不得让 AI 一个人干完一家公司的活。

另一边是你真正走进企业，发现很多项目连最基本的稳定性、权限管理、异常处理都没有解决。

卧槽，这种差距真的太明显了。

最近我自己也一直在折腾企业知识库、GEO 自动化、视频生产工作流，包括一些企业内部的软件系统。

做得越多，我反而越觉得：让 Agent 跑起来越来越容易了，让 Agent 真正跑进企业的业务流程里，才是最难的。

以前觉得接几个 API、调用几个工具、配置一套 Workflow，能把任务自动执行完，就算做出来一个挺不错的 AI 应用了。

但实际接触企业需求之后才发现，根本不是这么回事。

客户不关心你用了多少个 Agent，也不关心你调用的是 LangGraph、Dify 还是 Coze。

他只关心几个问题：原来三个人做的事情，现在能不能一个人完成？原来一天才能处理完的工作，现在能不能缩短到半小时？系统出错了怎么办？客户数据会不会泄露？后面谁来维护？

你技术架构画得再牛逼，业务价值交付不出来，在客户眼里可能就是一个高级玩具。

而且我发现，Agent 开发正在越来越接近传统的软件工程。

尤其是 RAG，很多人以为做知识库就是上传几个 PDF，调用 Embedding，往向量数据库里一存，再接个大模型就完事了。

真正做起来才知道，麻烦的东西全在后面。

文档更新了怎么办？不同版本的内容发生冲突怎么办？员工能不能查到自己没有权限看的文件？检索出来的证据不准确怎么办？模型开始胡说八道怎么办？

这些问题你不解决，模型再聪明也没用。

当然，不是所有 Agent 都需要 RAG，但只要涉及大量企业内部知识和数据，检索质量、权限控制和证据溯源就可能直接决定整个系统能不能用。

还有一点，我觉得现在特别多人忽略了。

AI 能帮你把代码写出来，不代表你就不需要懂软件工程了。

恰恰相反，以前你可能要花很多时间去写 Python、Java、SQL，现在 Codex 能帮你生成大量代码。

但系统怎么部署、接口怎么设计、任务失败怎么重试、数据怎么存储、并发怎么处理、日志怎么记录、线上怎么监控，这些工程责任不会因为 AI 会写代码就消失。

甚至因为代码生成速度太快了，系统质量的控制反而变得更加重要。

还有 Evals，我越来越觉得，做 AI 应用最忌讳的一件事，就是靠感觉验收。

今天改了几句 Prompt，问了五个问题，发现回答不错，就觉得自己优化成功了。

但真正到企业里，几百个员工、几千次调用、几十种业务场景，模型只要在关键任务上出现一次严重错误，就可能影响整个业务。

所以你必须知道任务成功率是多少、检索命中率怎么样、Tool 调用失败了多少次、每次任务花多少钱、哪些场景必须人工接管。

没有这些东西，所谓的优化，很多时候就是自己感动自己。

我现在甚至觉得，未来 AI 应用工程师之间最大的差距，可能不是谁会用更多的框架，而是谁能真正理解一个企业的业务，把需求拆解清楚，再用合适的技术把它稳定地实现出来。

这也是我为什么越来越关注 FDE 这个方向。

它不是让你坐在电脑前天天研究最新的模型，而是让你真正走进企业，弄清楚客户到底有什么问题，判断哪些值得用 AI 解决，再把系统交付出去。

当然，我自己也还在补这些工程能力，离真正成熟的企业级交付还有距离。

但至少方向越来越清晰了，AI 时代，会调用模型的人会越来越多，会开发 Agent 的人也会越来越多。

真正稀缺的，不是能够把 Demo 做得多么炫酷的人，而是能够对结果负责、对业务负责、对交付负责的人。

说到底，企业买的从来不是 Agent，企业买的是效率，是成本下降，是业务增长，是确定性。

谁能把这些东西真正交付出来，谁才有资格拿到下一阶段 AI 应用市场的钱。

会搭 Agent，只是入场券。能把 Agent 做成真正可用、可维护、可规模化的业务系统，才是竞争力。

text:
Chopin + Proof-Driven Development Kit from @GitHubNext and @MSFTResearch enable teams to ship AI-generated code to production without reviewing it line by line, with stronger assurance than code review and testing alone. 

Now in research preview ⬇️

quotedTweet.text:
How do you _guarantee_ your agent's code is correct? You prove it.

Introducing Proof Driven Development Kit (PDD Kit) from @MSFTResearch.

PDD Kit helps turn your plan into a formal spec, then proves the agent's code meets that spec for every input. No vibe verification. PDD Kit is integrated with @GitHubNext's Chopin, so you can plan as a team.

PDD Kit takes an app's login flow from intent to a verified pull request:

It discusses your code, infers your intent as it goes, and proposes a formal spec in Verus, a proof language for Rust.

Once you approve the spec, the Verus verifier automatically proves the code meets it.

Where proof isn't possible, it falls back to empirical verification with tests and computer-use agents (CUAs).

It works on Rust today. No new language, no change in how you produce the underlying code, making formal methods more accessible.

The goal is a verified software factory, where engineers review specifications instead of code.

Come see it in action at GitHub Universe, Oct 28–29. Swing by the Speakeasy and ask for GitHub Next!

text:
I’ve been thinking about this a lot lately and I want to hear what people think.

What happens to America’s housing crisis when flying cars are actually normal?

I don’t mean air taxis you book like an Uber. I mean your own vehicle in your driveway that can get you to the city in the air.

We’re millions of homes short in this country. But we’re not short on land. We’re short on land close to where the jobs are. That’s the real problem. Everyone is fighting over the same small circle around every city, and prices go through the roof.

In places like Boston and LA, more than half of what you pay for a home is just the land under it. In cheaper areas it’s more like 15 to 20%.

Now imagine that circle gets way bigger. A place that’s an hour and a half drive from the city could be a 25 or 30 minute flight. If you double how far people can reasonably commute, you don’t double the land. You get about 4 times as much. All of a sudden there’s a lot more room to build, and a lot more places where a normal family can afford a home.

That takes pressure off the cities too. Less competition for every apartment, fewer bidding wars and rents that aren’t climbing every year.

Most people don’t avoid living further out because they hate it. They avoid it because they feel stuck. Far from work, far from family, far from everything. Take away the drive and that feeling goes away.

It would bring life back to a lot of small towns too. Old mill and manufacturing towns all over the country were built for way more people than live there now. Bring people back and the restaurants, the shops and the local economy come back with them.

This stuff is already being built. Companies like Alef, Jetson, Pivotal and XPeng are working on personal flying vehicles right now, and some are already taking orders. Network tech like 6G is being designed so that the sky can handle a lot more traffic.

It’s not perfect. It’ll be expensive at first like every new thing, and there’s weather, noise and rules to figure out. We’d also need to make sure the people already living in those towns don’t get priced out. But I’d rather think about it now than get caught off guard.

I really believe that within 10 years, living an hour and a half outside the city won’t mean feeling stuck. It’ll just mean more space, a cheaper house and a real shot at owning one.

Am I crazy or do you see it too? Would you move further out if you could fly to work?

“If you want to generate alpha, you can’t be sharing all this information.”

“That interviewer needs to think and feel and act like you do. It needs to have all the context that you do.”

“We’re just making primary research faster, cheaper, and embedded. If I had to summarize the whole thing, that’s what Qualitate is doing.”

@S_Kadakia  has spent almost 20 years in primary research. He joined Tom DelVecchio at ETR in 2011 and ran buy-side survey work for six years, then built research and data products at 7Park Data and CB Insights. In 2023, as ChatGPT and voice capture crossed human parity, he founded Qualitate: an AI interviewer that runs 45- to 65-minute expert conversations autonomously, grounded in what he calls the fastest-growing AI-moderated interview library in the world. Crew Capital wrote the first $1 million check when no one else would fund a company building its own expert panel; this week @Qualitate announced a $25 million Series A led by Insight Partners, with net revenue retention over 300% and run-rate revenue up 10x in nine months.

Sagar walks through Qualitate’s two products: the proactive library its interviewer builds with its own capital and questions, and the private channel-check product (your questions, your interviewer, your library, your internal inputs, never mixed back in) that a couple dozen hedge funds have already moved their checks to. We get into why the architecture matters: grounding  over re-training for each new model, persistent memory so call five knows calls one through four, and transcripts structured like surveys so you can query them for time series instead of just searching.

“You can search through transcript files, but you can’t actually query that data. On Qualitate, you can actually query transcripts.”

“We don’t train or fine-tune anything. Because if you do that and the next version comes out, all of that work you just did goes to zero. We ground it.”

text:
Netflix $NFLX beat earnings. 

The stock still hit a 2-year low. 
EPS $0.87 vs $0.82 expected. Profit up 49%. Record $4.8B buyback.
And the stock is down nearly 30% this year.

Here’s why:

The market isn’t pricing last quarter. It’s pricing attention.

YouTube: free. No credit card, no commitment. You open it for one video and stay for an hour.

Netflix: pay first, then decide if it’s worth it. And every month you get to ask yourself if it still is.

YouTube is now 14.2% of all US TV viewing. Netflix is 7.8%. A year ago that gap was 4.6 points. Now it’s 6.4.

Netflix’s global viewing hours grew 2% in the first half of 2026.

Revenue growth looks similar for now (both ~11-13%). That’s the trap. 

Revenue is a lagging indicator. Attention is the leading one.

Free gets you the habit. The habit gets you the ad dollars, then the subscription upsell (YouTube Premium, TV).

Pay-first has to win you over every month, and Netflix is now building an ad tier to chase the attention it didn’t capture upfront. 
That ad forecast just got cut by $300M

Same lesson as Spotify. Own the habit first, monetize second.

The question for NFLX: is a falling share of attention a cyclical dip or a structural problem?

text:
AionUi showed up this week as an open-source cowork app that lets you run OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, and a handful of other agent CLIs from one interface, with a Leader and Teammate mode that delegates subtasks through its own MCP server. It's a solid build, and it's the fourth or fifth tool I've seen this year trying to solve the same problem: nobody wants four terminal tabs open just to compare how Claude Code and Codex handle the same bug.

The pattern across these tools is mostly the same shape. Claude Squad gives you a tmux session and a git worktree per agent. Sculptor does the same from a desktop app. Vibe Kanban did it as a kanban board, though it hasn't shipped a commit since April. Conductor is macOS only. What almost none of them touch is the part that actually breaks teams: what happens when two agents disagree, or one wants to run a command the other would veto.

That's the gap I built Campfire to close. It runs Claude Code, Codex, Goose, Aider, and OpenHands side by side in one browser tab, with permission voting across backends instead of trusting whichever agent asks first: majority rules approves, any single deny blocks, a 30 second timer keeps things moving. You can race the same task across every backend in isolated worktrees and see which one actually wins, replay a session afterward, and watch a cost dashboard show you which agent is burning your budget. It's open source, self-hosted, one command to try: bunx the-campfire.

https://t.co/WwOLZbMwgh
https://t.co/8NnCAiIUuL

quotedTweet.text:
🧭 AionUi is an open-source 24/7 Cowork app for working with AI agents from one cross-platform interface. It combines a built-in agent with support for OpenClaw, Hermes, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Qwen Code, Gemini CLI and many more, so you can move from a single chat to coordinated work on files, code, research, and scheduled tasks.

🛠️ What it does
• Gives agents controlled file read/write, web search, image generation, and MCP tool access.
• Runs multiple agents in parallel with independent context, or forms a Leader/Teammate team that delegates subtasks through a Team MCP Server.
• Offers a WebUI for remote access plus integrations such as Telegram, Lark, DingTalk, and WeChat.
• Includes a preview panel for 10+ formats, file organization helpers, document and spreadsheet workflows, and an extensible assistant/skills system.

✅ Practical uses & learning points
1) Create a personal or team Cowork workspace for coding, research, and document production.
2) Compare different CLI agents and model providers behind one UI while keeping each session isolated.
3) Schedule recurring data aggregation, report generation, file organization, or reminder tasks with cron, interval, or one-time triggers.
4) Study multi-agent orchestration: permissions, shared workspaces, ACP connections, MCP transports, skills, and human approval points.

⚙️ Getting started
Download the release for macOS, Windows, or Linux, or install on macOS with brew install aionui. Open the app, enter an API key for a supported provider, and start Coworking with the built-in agent. AionUi also supports local Ollama or LM Studio setups. For development, the Electron frontend works with the AionCore local backend; the repository is primarily TypeScript and includes the development guide for building both parts.

⚠️ License & security
AionUi is Apache-2.0 licensed. Treat API keys and service tokens as secrets, review each agent’s file and tool permissions, and require approval before enabling unattended or remote automation on sensitive workspaces.

🔗 Repository: https://t.co/MJsahlIwt7

🧭 AionUi is an open-source 24/7 Cowork app for working with AI agents from one cross-platform interface. It combines a built-in agent with support for OpenClaw, Hermes, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Qwen Code, Gemini CLI and many more, so you can move from a single chat to coordinated work on files, code, research, and scheduled tasks.

🛠️ What it does
• Gives agents controlled file read/write, web search, image generation, and MCP tool access.
• Runs multiple agents in parallel with independent context, or forms a Leader/Teammate team that delegates subtasks through a Team MCP Server.
• Offers a WebUI for remote access plus integrations such as Telegram, Lark, DingTalk, and WeChat.
• Includes a preview panel for 10+ formats, file organization helpers, document and spreadsheet workflows, and an extensible assistant/skills system.

✅ Practical uses & learning points
1) Create a personal or team Cowork workspace for coding, research, and document production.
2) Compare different CLI agents and model providers behind one UI while keeping each session isolated.
3) Schedule recurring data aggregation, report generation, file organization, or reminder tasks with cron, interval, or one-time triggers.
4) Study multi-agent orchestration: permissions, shared workspaces, ACP connections, MCP transports, skills, and human approval points.

⚙️ Getting started
Download the release for macOS, Windows, or Linux, or install on macOS with brew install aionui. Open the app, enter an API key for a supported provider, and start Coworking with the built-in agent. AionUi also supports local Ollama or LM Studio setups. For development, the Electron frontend works with the AionCore local backend; the repository is primarily TypeScript and includes the development guide for building both parts.

⚠️ License & security
AionUi is Apache-2.0 licensed. Treat API keys and service tokens as secrets, review each agent’s file and tool permissions, and require approval before enabling unattended or remote automation on sensitive workspaces.

🔗 Repository: https://t.co/MJsahlIwt7

PUBLIC SERVICE ANNOUNCEMENT FROM YOUR LOCAL CYBER SECURITY SPECIALIST

For those who don’t know what this recent PHP security vulnerability means:

This affects most public facing websites. 

These vulnerabilities can allow someone to gain access to most websites and their hosting server. That could give them access to sensitive information and/or creds. That is a serious problem.

Companies are working on patching this immediately. But if someone already got in, patching the vulnerability isn't enough. Backdoors could still be there and you can't take back already stolen data. 

The part I am most concerned about. Do these companies have the knowledge, staff, and information needed to properly investigate whether someone got in before they applied the fix? Most don't. 

You are going to hear things like "your data was encrypted" this does not automatically mean it was safe. If someone controls the service that can decrypt that information, or the attacker has plenty of time and resources on their hands, the information can be decrypted. 

This can also affect apps and other services that rely on these connections. How far an attacker can get depends on what those servers can access and how well the company has separated its systems. From many years of experience, most companies don't have good security posture.

FOR THE REGULAR NONTECHNICAL PERSON:

Don’t assume every account you have was hacked. This is a REALLY good time to pay attention and get your account security in order.

SO:

Keep an eye out for breach notices and unusual login activity. If you get an unexpected message telling you to reset your password, go to the company’s website or app directly. Don’t blindly trust or click links in emails. Fake security warnings will ramp up to take advantage of peoples fear.

Stop reusing passwords, ESPECIALLY THE SAME PASSWORD OR A VARIATION OF IT. Use a different password for each account, and turn on multifactor authentication wherever possible. Start with your email. If a company tells you your password was exposed, change it there and anywhere else you used the same or a similar one.

Being a regular person does not mean you’ll be ignored. A lot of account attacks are automated. Someone doesn’t need to know who you are to try your and a thousand other peoples stolen login on a hundred other websites simultaneously.

If you have ANY questions or need any help what so ever please let me know.
